EMPIRICAL RESEARCH • 20 OCTOBER 2026

Can Timestral trade?

A real 209M-parameter checkpoint, nine Yahoo Finance histories, three context lengths, and a confidence-aware simulated account.

209,312,256 parameters · FP32100 / 250 / 500 observations 200 calibration + 500 test originsNo real orders

The primary test does not establish a dependable trading edge.

4/9 instruments beat a zero-return forecast on MAE; 0/9 have a positive MAE improvement interval before multiple-testing adjustment. Confidence-sized accounts made money in 3/9 cases and beat passive holding in 3/9. Those counts do not establish statistical or prospective profitability.

4/9beat zero-return MAE
51.2%mean direction accuracy
3/9profitable sized accounts
2.57×largest observed exposure

This is historical research with a newly released pretrained model. The public training description does not establish exclusion of these histories, so this is not a certified unseen-data or prospective backtest. Model benchmark rankings are not trading evidence.

What happened to 100,000?

Primary context: 250 daily log returns. Every instrument gets a separate 100,000-unit account: INR for Indian equities and USD/INR, USD for U.S. instruments and EUR/USD or GBP/USD. These are quote-currency simulations, not a consolidated multi-currency account. The confidence strategy has a 3× ceiling; it does not automatically use 3×.

Is it a good forecast?

The primary target is the individual daily return two observations ahead. A positive MAE skill beats forecasting zero; a positive probabilistic skill beats quantiles from the trailing history. Return R² is negative in 9/9 primary instruments. The median raw 80% interval covers 79.4% of outcomes, and the calibrated median covers 80.2%: reasonable central uncertainty estimates can coexist with little useful directional information.

This experiment uses univariate zero-shot daily-return inputs and separate price-level inputs. The findings apply to this setup. Fine-tuning and richer inputs such as volume, cross-asset covariates or market events would require their own evaluation.

The price R² trap

A forecast can closely track the price level yet fail to improve on tomorrow’s price being today’s price. These independent price-level diagnostics use the latest 100 completed one-step origins, with fewer observed outcomes at longer horizons. For example, MSFT price R² is 0.968, yet its MAE is 0.57% worse than simply repeating the last price.

Does confidence deserve a larger bet?

Raw probabilities come from the model’s return quantiles. A regularized logistic map is fitted on 200 earlier examples and frozen for the entire test. It can reverse the raw signal when earlier data indicate an inverse relationship; negative coefficients in the calibration table expose that.

confidence = max(P(up), 1 − P(up))
conviction = clip((confidence − 0.55) / 0.15, 0, 1)
exposure = direction × min(cap, conviction × 10% / trailing annual volatility)

Below 55% confidence: cash. From 55–70%: increasing risk allocation. At 70% and above: full volatility-scaled allocation, capped at 1× or 3×. Trailing volatility uses 60 completed observations and a 1% floor. This mapping was fixed before results, not optimized on the test.

Marker size represents sample count. Empty confidence bands contain no supporting evidence. A 65% estimate that wins only 50% of the time is overconfident, not a reason to borrow more.

Is confidence adding information, or just reducing exposure?

Two diagnostic baselines were added during implementation: base_rate_sized sizes from the calibration period's constant up frequency, without model information; volatility_scaled_sign removes the confidence multiplier but keeps the calibrated direction and volatility target. These explanatory comparisons were not used to tune the strategy.

SPY illustrates the distinction: confidence sizing earns 4.04%, while sizing from the historical up frequency alone earns 3.90%. Most of that result does not require useful model-dependent confidence. USD/INR reaches 2.57× exposure but loses 2.31% after costs; a larger position does not repair a weak forecast.

Does more history help?

All three settings are reported. The 250-observation setting was selected before seeing performance; picking whichever setting won this test would require a new untouched evaluation.

Costs can erase the apparent edge

One-way execution costs: India 10 bps, U.S. 5 bps, EUR/USD and GBP/USD 2 bps, USD/INR 3 bps. Every entry, exit and rebalance is charged, including position drift. Financing is 8% annually on gross exposure above 1×; short borrow is 3% on short notional. Carry charges use calendar days. These are scenario assumptions, not broker quotes.

What does it forecast next?

The return signal predicts the individual daily return at observation +2. It waits one complete observation before entry. The latest-only calibration below is refreshed using the most recent 200 known test outcomes; this refresh never changes the historical performance table. Research exposure is a formula output, not a validated trade recommendation.

Price ranges above are raw marginal model intervals, not calibrated trading-risk limits. They do not include a joint path distribution or a promise that a whole future path remains inside the band. Horizons are trading observations, not calendar dates.

How to interpret the evidence

  1. Beat simple baselines first. A powerful general forecasting model may have little useful information about daily asset returns.
  2. Separate prediction from implementation. Better MAE does not automatically give better directional trades, and gross profit can disappear after turnover and borrowing.
  3. Check calibration before increasing exposure. Small calibration samples and regime changes make probability estimates uncertain. Low realized exposure may be the correct output.
  4. Demand forward evidence. Freeze the method and collect genuinely new outcomes after release before treating a historical winner as a deployable strategy.

Uncertainty intervals use 2,000 circular moving-block resamples of 20 observations. They are exploratory, conditional on the fitted calibration, and not corrected for all contexts, assets, horizons and strategies tested. They do not account for uncertainty in model training or deployment.

Additional limitations: selected surviving instruments; retrospective Yahoo adjustments; indicative FX daily quotes; no bid/ask or executable intraday data; no actual FX carry or cross-currency conversion; simplified funding; no borrow-availability or margin-call simulation; daily drawdowns miss intraday stress. Overnight Indian short positions and FX exposure require suitable tradable contracts. No missing outcomes are forward-filled and no returns are winsorized.

Reproduce and inspect

Checkpoint revision: 9874d252ab0aae16f7f7c999f98f98d6ad7d8365. Inference uses official code, FP32 weights and default symmetric averaging. The CPU and a custom Vulkan matrix-multiplication backend share the work. The latter passed a 36-origin check against CPU forecasts across price/return inputs and all contexts; the maximum difference was approximately 0.0013% of interval width. Integer quantization was rejected after a numerical check; none of these results use it.

Files alongside this report include every test prediction, account path, strategy metric, confidence bucket, latest forecast, source manifest and environment lock. PROTOCOL.md explains the predeclared design. Scripts can resume from forecast caches.
